mcqs.question: Why can't separate B-tree indexes on latitude and longitude efficiently answer "find everything within 2km of this point"?
options: B-trees cannot store decimal numbers like coordinates
Each index sorts only its own dimension, so neither alone captures the 2D relationship that makes points actually near each other
Latitude and longitude values are always too large to index
B-tree indexes can only be built on integer columns
mcqs.explanation: Proximity is a two-dimensional relationship; a 1D sorted index on one coordinate discards how it relates to the other, so a range scan on either alone still leaves distant points as candidates. B-trees handle decimals and large values fine — that isn't the limitation.

mcqs.question: What makes a quadtree different from a fixed-depth geohash grid?
options: A quadtree can only store one point per node
A quadtree only subdivides further where points are actually dense, adapting cell size to real data distribution
A quadtree ignores geographic coordinates entirely
A quadtree requires exactly four points per query
mcqs.explanation: Unlike a uniform grid, a quadtree keeps splitting only where points are dense, so sparse areas get large cells and dense areas get many small ones — adaptive to the actual data. It isn't limited to one point per node, and it still operates on real coordinates.

mcqs.question: A system needs to index delivery zone polygons (shapes with real area, not just points) and efficiently query which zones overlap a given area. Which structure fits best?
options: Plain geohashing of each polygon's center point only
A quadtree storing only point centroids
A single B-tree sorted by zone ID
An R-tree, since it groups objects — including shapes with extent — by bounding box for overlap queries
mcqs.explanation: R-trees are built around bounding boxes and naturally represent objects with real extent like polygons, letting a query skip any box that doesn't overlap the search area. Geohashing a centroid or storing just points loses the shape's actual extent, and a B-tree on ID doesn't capture spatial relationships at all.

mcqs.question: A geohash-based "nearby" search only queries geohashes sharing the exact prefix of the query point, and it's missing some points that are genuinely a few meters away. What's the fix?
options: Also query the neighboring cells around the target cell, then filter the combined candidates by actual distance
Increase the geohash string length to 20 characters
Switch to sorting results alphabetically instead of by distance
Store every point using two different geohash encodings
mcqs.explanation: Points near a cell boundary can land in an adjacent cell with a different prefix, so a correct nearby-search checks the target cell plus its neighbors before filtering by real distance. Lengthening the hash or double-encoding doesn't address the boundary problem, and sort order is unrelated.

mcqs.question: A ride-sharing query needs drivers within a 500m radius. Which geohash precision level is the best match, and why?
options: 5 characters, because coarser cells always mean faster queries
6-7 characters, because that cell size roughly matches the 500m radius, keeping the candidate set small without missing valid matches
It doesn't matter, since every geohash length returns the same candidates after filtering
20 characters, to guarantee maximum precision regardless of radius
mcqs.explanation: Matching cell size to the search radius keeps the target-plus-neighbor-cells candidate set small and relevant; a 5-character cell (~4.9km) is far bigger than needed and returns far more candidates than necessary, while an extremely long hash creates too many tiny cells for a 500m radius. Precision genuinely changes which cells and how many candidates you fetch.
